extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists and researchers interested in media freedom and Tunisia
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of censorship practices, laws, institutions, and illustrative cases in Tunisia from independence through the Ben Ali era and post‑2011 developments. Covers legal provisions, media-specific controls (books, newspapers, radio, TV, internet), technical filtering, and prominent prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantee with legal limitations (Article 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 8 of the Tunisian Constitution states 'the liberties of opinion, expression, the press, publication, assembly, and association are guaranteed and exercised within the conditions defined by the law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames freedom of expression as formally guaranteed but explicitly subject to conditions defined by law, implying that statutory limitations (criminal defamation, public order, religion, etc.) are lawful bases for restricting speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Code declaration of press freedom (Article 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 1 of the Press Code provides for 'freedom of the press, publishing, printing, distributing and sale of books and publications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as a formal statutory affirmation of press freedoms, but the article and subsequent text show such provisions coexisted with administrative controls and censorship practices (e.g., licensing, permits, seizures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative control of book distribution (Press Code receipt requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press Code requires a receipt from the Ministry of the Interior before distributing books in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical mechanism enabling pre‑distribution review or blocking of books; used to restrict publication and circulation of works on sensitive topics (religion, politics). Example: 40 books reportedly censored 1995–2005.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censoring or limiting foreign newspaper editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain editions of foreign newspapers critical of the regime (Le Monde, Libération, La Croix, Le Figaro) are often banned or censored; the regime authorized only a very limited number of editions of foreign newspapers to avoid accusations of censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational practice: entire editions can be stopped, some banned editions kept 'behind the counter' requiring special request. Examples: multiple censored editions of Le Monde, Libération blocked in 2007 after critical articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent bans on particular publications (satire example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publications such as Charlie Hebdo and Le Canard enchaîné are described as being banned on a permanent basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates targeted, lasting prohibitions applied to outlets judged unacceptable by authorities, especially satirical or strongly critical press.

rubrics_metrics.name: State monopoly and licensing in broadcast media
rubrics_metrics.description: The state exercises a monopoly on domestic television transmissions; a permit is required to establish a radio station and private radio stations do not independently report news. Electoral endorsements of candidates are not permitted in the private media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural controls over broadcast spectrum and licensing limit pluralism and independent reporting; explicit content restrictions (no electoral endorsements) regulate political speech in broadcast media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑2011 official proclamation of complete information freedom and institutional changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the 2011 ouster of Ben Ali the acting government proclaimed complete freedom of information and expression as a fundamental principle, abolished the information ministry, and removed filters on social networking sites such as Facebook and YouTube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents a policy shift away from prior controls; however, later examples show that freedoms declared can be partially rolled back via courts, military orders, or other measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal grounds used to block online content (military reputation, public order, minors/morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and tribunals ordered blocks on Facebook pages for attempting 'to damage the reputation of the military institution' and a court ordered the Tunisian Internet Agency to block porn sites on the grounds they posed a threat to minors and Muslim values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates the categories authorities invoke to justify online censorship: protection of military reputation, public order/stability, and protection of morality/minors; these grounds enable selective blocking even after formal liberalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical filtering and traffic controls used for large‑scale blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Ben Ali thousands of websites were blocked and peer‑to‑peer and FTP transfer were blocked using a transparent proxy and port blocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes concrete technical methods (transparent proxy, port blocking) used to implement censorship at scale, affecting categories like pornography, cached pages, conversion/translation services, and file transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization and imprisonment for online or critical expression (blasphemy, insulting religion, membership in illegal organisations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals were jailed for online activities or for content deemed insulting to religion or for membership in banned political organisations; examples include lengthy prison sentences for posting critical material or caricatures, and prosecutions for membership in 'illegal organisations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how laws (blasphemy, public order, membership/association offences) were applied to silence dissent; high‑profile cases cited (e.g., Ghazi Beji and Jabeur Mejri sentenced for Facebook posts) underscore severity and deterrent effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective enforcement and use of harassment tactics against critics and journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and opponents faced arrest, imprisonment, harassment (assaults, smear campaigns), administrative barriers to registering publications, and obstacles to distributing censored material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond formal bans, authorities used harassment, administrative denial (e.g., refusing to register Kalima), and media smear campaigns to suppress voices; these practices effectively limit media pluralism even absent explicit statutory prohibition.
